newsitem.title: INDIA: News Corp's STAR plans India DTH channel.
newsitem.headline: News Corp's STAR plans India DTH channel.

text.p: News Corp's loss-making Asian satellite broadcaster STAR TV plans to invest hundreds of millions of dollars in India's first direct-to-home (DTH) satellite pay channel, company officials said on Wednesday.

"The investment in this kind of business would range in the hundreds of millions of dollars. A lot would depend on the date of its launch and the number of channels," STAR's India chief executive officer Rathikant Basu told a news conference.
In the year to June 30, 1996, Hong Kong-based STAR's operating losses were estimated at around $80 million.
STAR TV's chief executive officer Gary Davey said he viewed the firm's losses as investments in a more profitable future.
"STAR TV's always been, in our minds, a very long-term proposition, and part of that long-term plan is DTH platforms," he told Reuters.
"We're on a growth curve that's working pretty much precisely to plan. We've had no shocks along the way, we don't like to call them losses, we call them investments," he said.

Basu said STAR can launch the new channel, to be called India Sky Broadcasting (ISkyB), only after the Indian government grants it a licence to use KU-band transponders. He said the company had already applied for the licence.

He said ISkyB aimed to reach only about 150,000 Indian customers by the end of its first year. Up to 20 million Indian homes subscribe to cable television, while state-run Doordarshan television reaches about 70 million.
Asked about returns on the firm's investment in ISkyB, Basu said: "I don't think the numbers are going to be very large, and it will take us some years before we break even."

Indian viewers would have to pay about 12,000 rupees ($335) as installation charges for ISkyB with a monthly subscription fee of 500 rupees, Basu said. Cable television installation costs about 500 rupees, with a subscription fee of some 100 rupees a month.
"We are not in competition with cable," Basu said. "I think there are a lot of people in India who want quality service and are willing to pay for it."
Davey said a PanAmSat Corp satellite would transmit the DTH service into India.
"We have already envisaged another satellite to be launched and parked next to PanAmSat as well, giving us virtually unlimited channel capacity," Davey said.

He said ISkyB would beam Fox Kids Network, STAR World, NBC, CNBC, entertainment channel UK TV Granada and financial news network Bloomberg Information TV, along with a history channel, a computer programmes channel and the first 24-hour Indian news channel.

He said the DTH satellite service would be able to reach subscribers in remote regions, and provide subscribers with greater viewing choice and superior audio and video quality compared with cable television. ($1 = 35.9 rupees)
